nameStory: This plant gets its name from John Macoun, a Canadian botanist who explored and catalogued plants across North America in the late 1800s. The 'everlasting' part comes from the papery, persistent flowers that keep their shape and color long after drying, making them popular in dried flower arrangements that seem to last forever.
description: Macoun's everlasting is a modest annual wildflower that grows 1-3 feet tall with a branching, upright stem. It's covered in soft, woolly hairs that give the entire plant a grayish-green, fuzzy appearance. The small whitish flowers cluster at the tips of branches in dense, rounded heads, blooming from late summer into fall. Like other members of the sunflower family, what looks like individual flowers are actually clusters of tiny flowers packed together.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel soft and woolly to the touch, with a grayish-green color from dense white hairs covering both surfaces

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, cream-colored to whitish flower heads clustered at branch tips, papery and dry-feeling even when fresh, with a faint sweet scent

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright annual plant 1-3 feet tall with multiple branches near the top, entire plant feels soft and cottony when brushed against

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Densely covered in white woolly hairs that rub off easily on fingers, leaving them feeling slightly fuzzy

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny seeds topped with fluffy white bristles that catch the wind, similar to dandelion seeds but much smaller

habitat: Look for Macoun's everlasting in disturbed soils, old fields, roadsides, and woodland clearings throughout New England. It prefers sandy or gravelly soils and thrives in areas with full sun to partial shade. You'll often find it growing alongside goldenrod, asters, and other late-season wildflowers in abandoned agricultural areas.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes of woolly leaves close to the ground, easily overlooked among other spring growth.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow taller and begin branching, developing their characteristic fuzzy appearance but not yet flowering.
seasonality.fall: Flowering period begins in late summer and continues through fall, when the distinctive whitish flower clusters become most visible.
seasonality.winter: Dried stems and seed heads may persist, with fluffy white bristles still visible on old flower heads if snow hasn't knocked them down.

funFact: The woolly hairs covering this plant aren't just for looks - they're actually a sophisticated water collection system that can capture moisture from fog and dew, allowing the plant to thrive in dry conditions where other plants would wilt.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with pearly everlasting, but Macoun's everlasting has much narrower leaves and tends to be more branched at the top. Remember: Macoun's has skinnier leaves and a more 'bushy' flower arrangement, while pearly everlasting has broader leaves and flowers in flatter clusters.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'everlasting,' this is actually an annual plant that dies each year, unlike some of its perennial relatives. The 'everlasting' refers only to how long the dried flowers maintain their appearance, not the plant's lifespan.
compareHints: Macoun's everlasting differs from its close relative sweet everlasting by having narrower, more linear leaves and a more openly branched flower arrangement. Sweet everlasting has broader, more spoon-shaped leaves and denser, more compact flower clusters. [Note: I'm somewhat uncertain about specific morphological differences between these two Pseudognaphalium species and recommend consulting current botanical references for definitive identification features.]

relatedSpecies.distinction: Sweet everlasting differs from its close relative Macoun's everlasting mainly in its preferred habitat and leaf shape - sweet everlasting has narrower leaves and grows in drier, sandier spots, while Macoun's everlasting prefers moister areas and has slightly broader leaves.
